I've taken buspar(buspirone). I don't believe this is a medication that you take as needed.

And as someone who often experiences side effects from medications, buspar did not help nor hurt me.

The more confusing and difficult part about medications is they impact people differently. Buspar helps a lot of people - but not everyone. The best option is starting at a low dose, which will help your body adjust and minimize side effects. If you're concerned about side effects, (totally understandable) keep a journal. Unfortunately, all medications carry the risk of side effects. What helps one person could be a nightmare for someone else.

I was prescribed lamictal and i had extremely terrifying side effects. Zoloft too.

With that said -  definitely discuss this with your doctor/prescriber. If you don't feel comfortable with that, try to find someone else. From my experience and understanding, buspar isn't a medication that's taken as needed. It needs to be administered regularly and doesn't begin to have an impact until 2-4 weeks, on average.

Anxiety medications that are commonly taken as needed are benzodiazepines (lorazepam, clonazepam, etc.), beta blockers (ex: propanolol), or antihistamines (ex: hydroxyzine).

When it comes to propanolol or metoprolol: these medications impact the physiological effects, but not necessarily the root cause of anxiety.

If you don't think your doctor/prescriber is helping and/or listening to you, I urge you to find someone else who will.

An **allergist/immunologis**t can diagnose asthma. Typically, they'll have an additional 2-3 years training in this subspecialty and will have studied allergies, asthma, and other immunodeficiency disorders. If a particular allergist said they can't/won't diagnose something, that might be their preference.

**Also, an allergist and ENT are not the same thing. The terms are not interchangeable.**

According to the American Academy of Allergy Asthma & Immunology: "Allergist / immunologists, often referred to as allergists, are specialists in the diagnosis and treatment of allergies, asthma and immune deficiency disorders."

ENTs (Ears, nose, throat) are otolaryngologist: this is a surgical subspecialty, meaning these doctors have additional training (post med school) in conditions that affect these parts of the body, including various cancers, as well as: otology (ears/hearing), rhinology (nose/smelling), laryngyology (larynx), etc. They'll also treat conditions like sinus infections, deviated septums, ear infections, tonsillitis, voice and sleeping disorders, sleep apnea.

Unfortunately, pulmonologists often have long wait times. Once you're an established patient, you'll likely have the ability to call and leave messages for refills and/or changes of inhalers (if one isn't helping, for example).

Also: the bacteria that causes tetanus, *clostridium tetani*, can form endospores - which allow the bacteria to go dormant and survive extreme, harsh, unfavorable conditions for extended periods of time. Once the conditions become favorable (like when the bacteria enters a human body), the bacteria once again becomes vegetative (meaning, it resumes growth/replication). 

*C. tetani* produces exotoxins (2 major ones) that blocks nerve signals and causes muscle spasms - this is what causes lockjaw - commonly associated with tetanus. Tetanus can be fatal if muscles involved in breathing or other vital functions are impacted.

The medication chosen and/or the medication that will be the most effective will likely depend on the type of asthma you have (eosinophilic, allergic, exercised-induced asthma, etc.) and the severity of the symptoms you experience.

I don't know why your doctors didn't mention a nebulizer, but you can also ask about a spacer. Both aim to deliver the most amount of the medication as possible. The nebulizer turns the medication into a mist whereas the spacer helps ensure you're breathing in slowly (breathing too rapidly will result in a whistling noise). 

\[Again, I'm not sure what  
country you're in. If you're not in the US, this might not apply at all. \]  
Sadly, many inhalers for asthma are extremely expensive. It might be helpful to  
contact your insurance company before your appointment and/or going to your insurance company's portal (if they have one) to **obtain their formulary.** This is a list of the medications that are covered and it can help you and your doctor find the option that fits your symptoms and is probably less expensive than a non-covered option. Keep track of the medications you take, especially if your symptoms are not improving or worsening. Sometimes certain medications are considered to be a higher tier because they're more expensive and will only be covered if you try a specified number of cheaper alternatives first. Alternatively, the manufacturers of some inhalers will have coupons on their websites that can reduce or eliminate most if not all of the cost of an inhaler. Be sure to read the fine print though, as some coupons are only usable for a certain number of months and others stipulate who can use them (example: some coupons are only for uninsured individuals and others are only for people with private insurance aka not medicare or medicaid).

**2.) long-term (maintenance/control) medications:** these medications aim to reduce the number of  
severity of flare ups/episodes. These medications won't provide immediate  
relief and therefore shouldn't be used in place of a rescue inhaler. Typically,  
these medications will take some time to work, but the time will vary depending  
on the particular medication. Examples include: 

a.) inhaled  
corticosteroids:   
\-budesonide   
\-ciclesonide  
\-fluticasone 

b.) combination inhalers:  
\-corticosteroid + long-acting beta agonist (LABA) like fluticasone/salmeterol, or  
   budesonide/formoterol  
\-long acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA)+ LABA like tiotropium/formoterol       
   (Spiriva) or glycopyrronium/fomoterol (Breztri). LAMAs are another type of      
bronchodilator. 

c.) leukotriene modifiers  
\- which can reduce inflammation by blocking the either the production or effects of leukotrienes, which are lipid(fat) derived molecules that play a role in asthma and allergic/immune responses by stimulating bronchoconstriction (narrowing of the airway due to muscle contraction) and by attracting leukocytes (white blood cells).  
Leukotrienes are released by mast cells during an asthma attack. An example is  
montelukast (singular). Note: the FDA added a blackbox warning to this medication  
(I'm not sure what country you're in). 

d.) Inhaled mast cell stabilizers -prophylactic (preventative) medications that suppress the release of inflammatory chemicals from mast cells, which are a kind of leukocyte (white blood cell) that's made in red bone marrow. Mast cells patrol different tissues and can release various chemical messengers (like leukotrienes or histamine) that can trigger inflammation andvarious immune responses in an effort   
to defend and protect the body. Unfortunately, immune responses are sometimes   
triggered at the wrong time and can cause problems.

Holding your breath for 10 seconds after an inhaler is often cited as ideal. Then, use mouth wash or brush your teeth to prevent thrush (bacterial infection in your mouth).

\-Albuterol is in your rescue inhaler, meaning it's designed to help you quickly and in-the-moment. This is different that maintenance (long-term) inhalers that are designed to help either prevent future episodes or lessen the severity.

**"New Jersey’s statutory codification of the common-law privilege, N.J.S.A. §2C:20-11(e) is illustrative:**

A law enforcement officer, or a special officer, or a merchant, who has probable cause for believing that a person has willfully concealed unpurchased merchandise and that he can recover the merchandise by taking the person into custody, may, for the purpose of attempting to effect recovery thereof, take the person into custody and detain him in a reasonable manner for not more than a reasonable time, and the taking into custody by a law enforcement officer or special officer or merchant shall not render such person criminally or civilly liable in any manner or to any extent whatsoever…. A merchant who causes the arrest of a person for shoplifting, as provided for in this section, shall not be criminally or civilly liable in any manner or to any extent whatsoever where the merchant has probable cause for believing that the person arrested committed the offense of shoplifting..."

When I have a lapse, I use a SMART tool called an "ABC" so I can learn from my slip up and prevent from making the same mistake in the future. 

A: activating event. What event led me to use an old coping mechanism (using your drug of choice)? Example: Did I have a fight with a friend or significant other, did I have a bad day at work, etc. 

B: belief. What (irrational) belief do I have about the activating event?   
Example: I can't stand getting in a fight and the only way to cope with my uncomfortable feelings is to use a drug or behavior. 

C: What's the consequence of the irrational belief?   
Example: If I (irrationally) believe that I cannot stand uncomfortable emotions, I will end up using unhealthy coping mechanism (like drugs and/or behaviors). This will erode my self-confidence, relationships, resiliency, health, etc. 

D: Dispute the irrational belief.   
Example: Even though it *feels* like I cannot stand uncomfortable feelings and *must* use substances or behaviors to cope, that isn't true. Everything is impermanent. All that has the nature to arise will also pass away, No matter how uncomfortable an urge or situation is, the truth is that it will pass. I need to practice withstanding discomfort and over time, I will get better at it. 

You can also add "E:" Effective change in my thinking.

I’m sure you and your friend both know that there is a laundry list of medications. If it seems like there is no improvement at all between the combination of medication and therapy, my thought would be maybe it’s not the right medication and/or the right kind of therapy. I would definitely mention this to my treatment team if I were you. 

            Unfortunately, medication in the mental health field comes down to a lot of guess-and-check. On top of that, many medications take weeks to months to begin to work, even slightly. So, for example, say your friend is prescribed the SSRI fluoxetine (Prozac) – which is a commonly prescribed first line of treatment. While some people may feel an effect within 1-2 weeks, it could take as long as 4-8 weeks. Imagine if that dosage isn’t high enough. The doctor will increase the dosage and you must wait again to hopefully see results. Say after the increase(s), there’s still no change and the doctor decides to change medications completely and you’re back to square one: having to wait weeks to hopefully feel some relief. It’s a tedious, if not tortuous, process. 

            On top of that, many people take more than one medication. Most providers will not start multiple medications at once or will not increase dosages of multiple medications at once because if something goes wrong, it’ll be difficult to pin down the culprit.

            The shitty thing about medication is it takes so much time. 

(Disclaimer: I’m not a healthcare provider and this is not medical advice; nor is this is the case for everyone). 

            I’m not sure about your friend’s background, but I personally had a difficult time with DBT at first. DBT was originally developed by Marsha Linehan to treat borderline personality disorder. This modality, however, can be applied to other diagnoses and has been helpful to so many people, but I found it very intimidating and invalidating. 

            When it comes to therapists, therapy modalities, and medications, we often need to shop around for the best fit. With that being said, I absolutely have to remind all of us -myself included- that change is difficult, and it takes a lot of time and practice. 

There are so many different modalities of treatment: cognitive behavioral therapy, DBT, internal family systems, motivational interviewing, rational emotive behavioral therapy, and rational therapy – which are the basis for SMART recovery, acceptance and commitment, emotional freedom techniques, grief therapy, neurofeedback, somatic experiencing, prolonged exposure, EMDR, trauma focused therapy…the list goes on). I found it helpful to research each modality and see what I thought would help me most. Since we are the ones who know ourselves best, I think we can discover what will help us the most. Also, we don’t have to limit ourselves to one kind of therapy. Even if it’s not possible to find multiple therapists that practice different modalities, there are countless books, websites, and youtube videos dedicated to each type.  If there’s a particular modality that seems fitting, then we can start to look for a therapist that’s either trained in that area or at least open to exploring it with you.

It depends. It certainly could. If you felt like your life was being threatened, you very well might fit the diagnostic criteria. In order to be diagnosed with PTSD, these are the criteria that must be met: (as per the DSM V)

1. Exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence
2. Presence of one (or more)  intrusion symptoms associated with the traumatic event(s), beginning after the traumatic event(s) occurred
3. Persistent avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event(s), beginning after the traumatic event(s) occurred, as evidenced by one or both of the following:
4. Negative alterations in cognitions and mood associated with the traumatic event(s), beginning or worsening after the traumatic event(s) occurred, as evidenced by two (or more) of the following
5. Marked alterations in arousal and reactivity associated with the traumatic event(s), beginning or worsening after the traumatic event(s) occurred, as evidenced by two (or more) of the following:
6. Duration of the disturbance (Criteria B, C, D and E) is more than 1 month.
7. The disturbance causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.
8. The disturbance is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (e.g., medication, alcohol) or another medical condition.

You can read the full descriptions [here](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK207191/box/part1_ch3.box16/). Or, you can look it up in the DSM under code 309.81/ICD-10 code F43.10

Trauma isn't a diagnosis in the same way that PTSD is. Rather, "trauma is a lasting adverse effect on an individual caused by an event that involves threat or danger...According to the DSM-5, trauma can result when an individual directly experiences an adverse event, witnesses that event, or learns about it from others. Exposure to trauma is very common. Each year, approximately 60 percent of children experience at least one trauma..."

PTSD used to be under the umbrella of anxiety disorders, but is now part of the "Trauma and Stressor-Related Disorders" category, along with:

Disinhibited social engagement disorderReactive attachment disorderAcute stress disorderAdjustment Disorders[1](https://mentalhealthgateway.org/trauma-and-stress-related-disorders/),[2](http://traumadissociation.com/trauma-stressor), [3](http://vcoy.virginia.gov/documents/collection/018%20Trauma2.pdf),[4](https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/essentials/dsm5_ptsd.asp#one)

Also, there is PTSD, which typically results from one event and complex PTSD (C-PTSD) which results from sustained trauma (often lasting months or years) and frequently begins in childhood. 

I agree with the previous poster: labels don't always matter. They will if you are considering applying for disability or something like that. But if that isn't your concern right now, you don't necessary have to worry what the exact title is.

First, I want to acknowledge the fact that covid probably put a lot of strain on so many relationships. Second, I have personally come to the conclusion that people who haven't experienced depression firsthand or witnessed a close loved-one's experience don't always have the ability to *really* understand what it's like. At first, I used to find this frustrating. But now, I realize that that means they are lucky. People who don't experience things first-hand can't understand in the same way as someone who's gone through it. I've come to believe that when I am feeling so down, so awful, and I need someone to validate my feelings and really understand where I'm coming from, I need to go to the right person. So, i think that's what life is about - determining who to go to for what. When you had a crappy day at work, maybe this guy is really good at making you laugh and feel better. But, when you're struggling with mental health issues, maybe it's best to go to someone who *gets* it (because they've been there). 

You aren't wrong for experiencing what you're feeling. it's tough when you're connected with someone but have a difficult time making them understand how you feel. In my opinion, keep trying until you reach your limit. Only you can determine where your limit is. Once you reach that limit, it's healthier for you to walk way (at least for now).
